paper.title: The division of parental leave: Empirical evidence and policy design
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability (p. 18): 'The authors do not have permission to share data.' Supplementary material is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpubeco.2024.105202. No Statistics Denmark project reference is given.

registers.role: treatment and outcome (weeks of parental leave), sample frame
variables_mentioned: amount of parental leave benefits received by each parent-child observation
whether the benefits are paid out to the parent or to the employer
start and end dates of the leave spell

registers.name_in_paper: monthly earnings data for the universe of Danish employees
registers.role: controls and construction (weekly earnings, wage rates, individual replacement rates, firm linkage)

registers.name_in_paper: administrative registers for the full population in Denmark, linked at the individual level via personal identification numbers
registers.role: linkage, demographics, education, firm and sector characteristics
variables_mentioned: employment sector of both parents (central, regional or local government; private sector)

registers.name_in_paper: Statistics Denmark (2020), Earnings by sex, components, salary earners, salary, sector, occupation and time (LONS20)
registers.role: external benchmark (average hourly wage rate of DKK 257 used to compute the effective replacement rate)

registers.name_in_paper: Statistics Denmark (2024), Cohabiting parents leave before birth and in the first year of life of the child (BARLOV1)
registers.role: external validation of the simulated reform effects against the actual 2022 Danish earmarked-leave reform

linkages: Several administrative registers linked at the individual level via personal identification numbers
Parents linked to each other as couples; each birth is one observation (a parent-child combination), so parents may enter multiple times
Individuals linked over time to other family members
Workers linked to firms; co-worker groups defined as firm-year cells, and where too few co-workers exhaust their compensation, as industry-year cells (6-digit, 740 groups; 5-digit, 127 groups)

sample.unit_of_observation: birth (parent-child combination); a couple observed at one birth
selection_rules: + No close births (exclude parents having a subsequent child within 15 months): 404,860 births
+ Parents in stable employment pre-birth (continuously employed in the same firm in the 3 months prior to birth): 213,658 births
+ Parents not on non-birth-related public benefits in the 3 months prior to birth (pregnancy-related benefits excepted): 194,217 births
+ Parents in parental leave data: 187,755 births (final sample)
sample.n_individuals: 242,915 mothers and 211,623 fathers individually fulfil the restrictions (Table 1, columns 2 and 3); the final sample requires couples to fulfil them jointly

construction_notes: The number of parental leave weeks is computed from the start and end dates of the leave spell; the total benefits paid out are used to calculate individual replacement rates, and the number of weeks with full wage compensation is computed from the amount of benefits paid to the employer.
The measure of parental leave includes all leave taken in the first two years after childbirth.
The analysis focuses on the division of the 32 weeks of shared parental leave, excluding the 14 weeks of maternity leave and the 2 weeks of paternity leave.
All monetary amounts are scaled to 2019 levels (EUR 1 ~ DKK 7.5); the benefit cap is DKK 4355 per week at the 2019 level.

Individual rights to wage compensation (z-bar_ij) are not observed and are imputed: in the public sector from the 6-6-6 model (6-7-6 from 1 April 2015) and the public sub-sectors of both parents; in the private sector from co-workers via equation (2) (the mode weeks of wage compensation among co-workers who exhaust with weakly more compensation), using firm-year cells where possible and industry-year cells otherwise.

Potential earnings growth is computed from a Mincer regression of log earnings on education level, field of study and labor market experience estimated on men only; it is the difference between predicted log earnings given pre-birth education and experience and given that experience plus 5 years.
Median leave is measured within 6-digit industry groups (740 groups).
In the policy simulations, taxes are computed as a flat 40% tax on all income, and net transfers include both public transfers and the wage compensation formally paid for by firms.
The model-fit simulations are based on 200 random pairs of alpha_im and alpha_if for each household; the estimation approximates the double integral over preferences with Gauss-Hermite quadrature.
In the counterfactual simulations the 14 weeks of maternity leave and 2 weeks of paternity leave are maintained and their take-up is not shown.

claims.statement: Households' marginal willingness to pay for an additional week of the father's shared parental leave, expressed as a percentage of weekly household earnings, has an average intercept at zero leave of 12.0.

treatment.label: An additional week of the father's take-up of the 32 weeks of shared parental leave (l_if)

register_source.value: Spell data on the use of parental leave covering parents of children born between 2008 and 2015, linked to monthly earnings data for the universe of Danish employees; the paper names no Statistics Denmark register code

definition.value: Weeks of the 32 weeks of shared parental leave taken by the parent; the number of parental leave weeks is computed from the start and end dates of the leave spell, and the measure includes all leave taken in the first two years after childbirth

timing.value: Leave taken in the first two years after childbirth; the marginal decision to transfer leave between parents falls in the last half of the shared parental leave, when the child is typically 8-12 months old

outcome.label: Fathers' marginal willingness to pay for parental leave at zero leave, MWTP(l = 0), as a percentage of weekly household earnings

definition.value: Average over the sample of the intercept of the father's marginal willingness to pay curve evaluated at zero leave, beta_if*alpha_if, computed from equation (4) and the parameter estimates in Table A.I of the Online Appendix

timing.value: Preference parameter evaluated for the birth in question; MWTP is expressed per week of the 32 weeks of shared parental leave, taking the other parent's leave as given

units.value: percent of weekly household earnings

estimand.target_population: the entire estimation population of Danish dual-parent households with a birth 2008-2015 (Table 4 reports averages for the entire population and selected sub-samples)
estimand.time_horizon: all leave taken in the first two years after childbirth
estimand.formal_query: E[ MWTP_ij(l_im, l_if) ] over the estimation sample, with MWTP as in equation (4)

population.description: Danish dual-parent households with a birth in 2008-2015 in which both parents were in stable pre-birth employment, not on non-birth-related public benefits pre-birth, and observed in the parental leave spell data (187,755 births)
population.selection: Births 2008-2015; excludes births where the parents have a subsequent child within 15 months; both parents in stable employment (continuously employed in the same firm in the 3 months prior to birth) and not on non-birth-related public benefits in those 3 months; both parents present in the parental leave data; couples must jointly fulfil the restrictions (414,248 -> 187,755 births).

identification.source_of_variation: Sharp kinks in the household budget set created by the Danish two-tier parental leave system: the exhaustion of each parent's individual, firm-provided wage compensation and the joint exhaustion of the 32 weeks of shared public parental leave benefits

key_assumptions.assumption: Parents react to parental leave reforms only through the reform's effect on the household budget set; no peer effects, norm effects or other general equilibrium responses
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 9 bin scatter of publicly employed fathers' bunching against the share of co-workers with the same right to wage compensation (slope -.0172, s.e. .0177); firm fixed effects reduce the variance in fathers' take-up by only 12%

implies_edges.to: parent's take-up of shared parental leave

key_assumptions.assumption: Households maximise u_i(l_im, l_if, c_i) subject to the budget constraint (1) and parents' revealed preferences are taken at face value

formal.as_written: c_i = B(l_im, l_if | S_i) + sum_{j in m,f} w_ij (T - l_ij)

key_assumptions.assumption: Quadratic utility, which translates the bunching response into a linear marginal willingness to pay curve
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 14 notes the functional form is largely inconsequential for small policy reforms but matters further from the initial policy setting

formal.as_written: MWTP_ij(l_im, l_if) = beta_ij ( alpha_ij - l_ij ) + rho_i l_i-j

key_assumptions.assumption: (alpha_im, alpha_if) follows a bi-variate normal distribution; the key requirement is that the distribution of alpha is smooth
key_assumptions.supported_by: Validated by comparing the simulated and observed distributions of leave outside the kink points (Figs. 4-6)

key_assumptions.assumption: Parents who take some leave without wage compensation must first have exhausted their individual right to wage compensation (z-bar_ij = z_ij if l_ij > z_ij); for the rest the right is imputed as the mode among co-workers who exhaust with weakly more compensation
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imputation applied to the public sector reproduces the collective-agreement rules for more than 90% of parents (Figure A.IV)

key_assumptions.assumption: Including pre-birth job characteristics of the parents in X_i controls for the selection of parents into firms with more or less generous wage compensation

lhs: individual right to wage compensation (position of the kink)
given: pre-birth job characteristics of the parents (X_i)

implies_edges.from: pre-birth job characteristics of the parents (X_i)
implies_edges.to: parent's take-up of shared parental leave

threats_discussed: General equilibrium effects, such as peer effects in leave take-up or changing norms
Within-firm peer effects possibly driving the observed bunching rather than the change in economic incentives
Measurement error in the imputed individual right to wage compensation (z-bar_ij), which works as classical measurement error and biases the estimated responsiveness towards zero
Functional form assumptions matter when moving further away from the initial policy setting
Revealed preferences taken at face value: externalities (signaling, norm effects) and ad hoc planner motives are not captured

heterogeneity.finding: Table 4 also reports sub-sample averages. Fathers: public sector 24.8 / -3.1 / 7.8; private sector 8.4 / -3.2 / 1.5; university education 15.0 / -2.8 / 2.6; first-time parent 12.7 / -3.3 / 2.7; female primary earner 14.0 / -3.3 / 3.0; high expected wage growth 13.6 / -3.1 / 2.5 (intercept / slope / average). Mothers: public sector 60.9 / -1.6 / 17.4; private sector 58.8 / -1.5 / 17.3; university education 55.3 / -1.5 / 16.8; first-time parent 61.0 / -1.6 / 17.8; female primary earner 62.2 / -1.6 / 19.2; high expected wage growth 58.5 / -1.5 / 17.8.

heterogeneity.dimension: fathers vs mothers
heterogeneity.finding: There are large differences between fathers and mothers, reflecting that mothers take significantly more leave than fathers, but also between fathers employed in the public and private sectors.

heterogeneity.dimension: across subgroups generally
heterogeneity.finding: We find limited heterogeneity across subgroups. (p. 9)

heterogeneity.dimension: mother primary earner, university degree, high expected wage growth
heterogeneity.finding: We see less heterogeneity when splitting the sample by whether the mother is the primary earner in the couple, or by whether the parent has a university degree or high expected wage growth. The estimates for fathers in these subgroups all lie above, but close to the population average. (p. 10)

heterogeneity.dimension: interpretation of the sub-sample differences
heterogeneity.finding: Hence, while these differences are not necessarily causal, they suggest that differences in the willingness to pay for parental leave is driven more by intrinsic preferences and less by, e.g., career concerns. (p. 10)

evidence.annotation: Fig. 4. Model fit: Fathers’ take-up of shared parental leave. Notes: The figure shows the actual and simulated distributions of fathers’ take-up of the 32 weeks of shared parental leave, split by the father’s sector and right to wage compensation. Fig. 5. Model fit: Mothers’ take-up of shared parental leave. evidence.annotation: Fig. 3. Observed take-up of shared parental leave. Notes: The figure shows the raw distributions of parents’ take-up of the shared parental leave. Panels A and B show the distributions for two groups of parents defined by the fathers’ rights to wage compensation (either 6 or 10 weeks). ... evidence.how: Fig. 3 prints β̂ as a positive number; the paper describes β as the slope of the marginal willingness to pay curve, with 'a small number implies a flat willingness to pay curve and larger responsiveness of parents', and the text reads the estimates as willingness to pay that FALLS by 3%-5% per additional week of leave. The sign of the relationship between own leave and marginal willingness to pay is therefore negative, while the transcribed point estimate is the printed positive magnitude β̂ = 4.8. In the model MWTP = beta(alpha - l) + rho*l_-j, so dMWTP/dl = -beta, consistent with the negative slopes printed in Table 4.

evidence.how: Fig. 3 prints β̂ as a positive number; the paper describes β as the slope of the marginal willingness to pay curve, with 'a small number implies a flat willingness to pay curve and larger responsiveness of parents', and the text reads the estimates as willingness to pay that FALLS by 3%-5% per additional week of leave. The sign of the relationship between own leave and marginal willingness to pay is therefore negative, while the transcribed point estimate is the printed positive magnitude β̂ = 3.7. In the model MWTP = beta(alpha - l) + rho*l_-j, so dMWTP/dl = -beta, consistent with the negative slopes printed in Table 4.

evidence.annotation: Fig. 8. The Effects of earmarked leave under different policy settings. Notes: The figure shows the simulated outcomes of introducing 1-12 weeks of earmarked parental leave in four different policy settings. In the simulations with fixed total leave, we keep the total leave at 32 weeks and thus let the earmarked leave reduce the shared leave. In the simulations with fixed shared leave, we extend the total leave by the number of earmarked weeks. In all simulations, we implement a uniform replacement rate of either 50% or 100% for both parents and for the entire duration of public parental leave.

Fig. 4. Model fit: Fathers’ take-up of shared parental leave. Notes: The figure shows the actual and simulated distributions of fathers’ take-up of the 32 weeks of shared parental leave, split by the father’s sector and right to wage compensation.

Fig. 5. Model fit: Mothers’ take-up of shared parental leave. Notes: The figure shows the actual and simulated distributions of mothers’ take-up of the 32 weeks of shared parental leave, split by the father’s sector and right to wage compensation.

evidence.annotation: Fig. 9. Correlation between likelihood of bunching and co-workers’ incentives. Notes: In this figure we exploit the heterogeneity in wage compensation between co-workers in the public sector created by the 6-6-6(7) model described in Section 3.1 and explore the extent to which individual behavior is affected by the behavior of co-workers. ... The figure shows a bin scatter plot of the correlation between publicly employed fathers’ likelihood of bunching at the exhaustion of their individual weeks of wage compensation and the share of his co-workers who have the same right to wage compensation. We control for the father’s own wage compensation and sector. If the bunching at kink points was primarily driven by peer effects, we would expect a positive correlation, as more co-workers with similar rights to wage compensation should reinforce the take-up of that particular number of weeks on parental leave. Printed in the plot: Slope = -.0172 (.0177)

evidence.how: The printed slope -.0172 with standard error .0177 is smaller than its standard error, and the paper reads it as 'little correlation'; the estimate is therefore recorded as not statistically significant at conventional levels.

population.selection: Births 2008-2015; excludes births where the parents have a subsequent child within 15 months; both parents in stable employment (continuously employed in the same firm in the 3 months prior to birth) and not on non-birth-related public benefits in those 3 months; both parents present in the parental leave data; couples must jointly fulfil the restrictions (414,248 -> 187,755 births).

identification.source_of_variation: Application of the Danish parental leave benefit rules to each household's observed earnings and rights to wage compensation

key_assumptions.assumption: The marginal cost of reallocating leave can be computed from the benefit rules of Section 3.1 together with the imputed individual rights to wage compensation
key_assumptions.supported_by: Model fit of the simulated against the observed distribution of the marginal cost (Fig. 6)

key_assumptions.assumption: Parents who take some leave without wage compensation must first have exhausted their individual right to wage compensation (z-bar_ij = z_ij if l_ij > z_ij); for the rest the right is imputed as the mode among co-workers who exhaust with weakly more compensation
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imputation applied to the public sector reproduces the collective-agreement rules for more than 90% of parents (Figure A.IV)

threats_discussed: Measurement error in the imputed individual right to wage compensation
robustness_checks: Model fit of the simulated and observed distributions of the marginal cost of father's leave (Fig. 6)

estimator.value: Descriptive: cumulative distribution of the computed marginal household cost of transferring one week of leave from the mother to the father

estimation.specification: Fig. 6, Panel A (households where the father does not exhaust his wage compensation)

sample_n.value: households where the father does not exhaust his wage compensation (around 45% of fathers); no count printed

source_table.value: Fig. 6, Panel A (page 13), with the 90% figure stated in the text on page 10

heterogeneity.dimension: whether the father exhausts his wage compensation (Fig. 6 Panels A and B)
heterogeneity.finding: In Panel B, where the marginal cost of reallocating leave is given by the difference in weekly earnings of the father and mother, the majority of households face a positive cost of reallocating leave.

evidence.panel: A: Fathers with Remaining Wage Compensation
evidence.annotation: Fig. 6. Model fit: Marginal cost of father’s leave. Notes: The figure illustrates the marginal household cost of transferring one week of leave from the mother to the father in the data and simulated from the model. The marginal cost is calculated using the benefit rules described in Section 3.1 and expressed relative to the weekly household pre-birth earnings. Panel A shows the distribution for households where the father does not exhaust his wage compensation (lif < z̄if), while Panel B shows the distribution for households where the father exhausts his wage compensation (lif ≥ z̄if). Around 45% of fathers do not exhaust their right to wage compensation.

theory_referenced: gender identity norms (Ichino et al., 2022; Giommoni and Rubolino, 2022)

prior_findings_compared.citation: Ichino et al. (2022); Giommoni and Rubolino (2022)
prior_findings_compared.as_stated: they reveal a strong willingness to pay for this gender traditional allocation of leave, which aligns with findings in other policy settings (Ichino et al., 2022; Giommoni and Rubolino, 2022).

anchor_quote.text: In Panel A, 90% of households could increase their disposable income by reallocating parental leave from the mother to the father with a median increase of just below 20% of weekly household earnings.
